tagline: Islands of rice, mangroves, and hippos
overview:
Guinea-Bissau is a small country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, wedged between Senegal and Guinea, about the size of Maryland and Delaware combined. Its coast is a maze of wide river estuaries, tidal creeks, and mangrove swamps, and offshore lie the Bijagós Islands, an archipelago of about 88 islands where only a couple dozen are inhabited. The capital, Bissau, is a low-rise port city on the Geba River estuary.

Around two million people live in Guinea-Bissau. Portuguese is the official language, but most people speak Upper Guinea Creole, a Portuguese-based creole known as Kriol, along with Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, and other languages. Roughly half of the people are Muslim, with large Christian and traditional-religion communities. It is one of the poorest countries in the world; farmers grow rice in the tidal flats and cashews, the main export, on the higher ground. The country is a republic, but coups and political disputes have troubled it since independence from Portugal in 1974.
landAndNature: Guinea-Bissau is flat and low, rising only to about 300 meters in the far east, and much of the coast floods at high tide. Rivers like the Geba, Corubal, and Cacheu spread into broad estuaries lined with mangrove forests that shelter fish, oysters, and manatees. The Bijagós Islands are a UNESCO biosphere reserve where saltwater hippos swim between islands and even wade in the ocean, and where green sea turtles lay eggs on Poilão island, one of the most important nesting beaches in the Atlantic. Inland savanna and woodland hold chimpanzees, monkeys, and antelope in the Cantanhez forests. Millions of migrating shorebirds arrive each winter from Europe. The climate is hot with a heavy rainy season from June to October.
peopleAndCulture: The Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Papel, and Manjaco are the largest peoples, and the Bijagó islanders keep distinct traditions, including a society where women have great authority and choose their husbands. Rice is the staple, grown in flooded paddies and served with fish, palm oil, or peanut sauce; cashew fruit is eaten fresh, and its nuts pay for school fees. Gumbe music blends Creole rhythms with guitars and drums, and Carnival in Bissau fills the streets with masks made of papier-mâché and dancers in raffia costumes. Wrestling and soccer are popular sports. Bijagó ceremonies feature carved masks of bulls, sharks, and sawfish, and village elders hold great respect. Many Bissau-Guineans have relatives in Portugal and Senegal.
history: The region was part of the Mali Empire's influence and the Kaabu kingdom of the Mandinka before Portuguese ships arrived in the 1440s. Portugal set up trading posts at Cacheu and Bissau that shipped enslaved people to the Americas, especially Cape Verde and Brazil, but controlled only the coast until the early 1900s. A guerrilla war for independence led by Amílcar Cabral began in 1963 and freed most of the countryside; Cabral was assassinated in 1973, and Portugal recognized independence in 1974. Guinea-Bissau's independence helped topple Portugal's dictatorship. Since then the country has suffered several coups, a civil war in 1998 and 1999, and the assassination of a president in 2009, and it has struggled with drug trafficking through its islands. Elections continue despite the turmoil.
funFacts: The hippos of the Bijagós Islands are among the only ones in the world that regularly swim in salt water and walk on ocean beaches.
Cashew nuts make up more than 90 percent of the country's exports, and the cashew harvest sets the rhythm of the year.
Guinea-Bissau's war of independence helped spark the 1974 revolution that ended dictatorship in Portugal.
Poilão island in the Bijagós is one of the most important green turtle nesting sites in the entire Atlantic Ocean.
In Bijagó culture, women traditionally choose their husbands and can also end a marriage by moving the man's belongings out.
